A backtest is a claim about the past, not a promise about the future. Tune enough parameters against one history and you find settings that flatter it by memorising its noise instead of its edge. The guard is walk-forward testing: optimise on one window, run it on the next window the fit never saw, and roll. If good numbers survive only inside the data they were tuned on, you have described last year, not built a process for next year.
A backtest optimised hard enough will fit the noise of its own history; the guard is a walk-forward test on data it never saw

A block explorer is a public index that lets you look up blocks, transactions, addresses and contract activity on a blockchain. It shows what the chain recorded — amounts, timestamps, status and event logs — so you can verify a transaction independently of any platform own dashboard. Explorers reflect on-chain data only; they do not reveal off-chain balances or internal ledgers.

A block explorer is a searchable index over a public chain, and every field on the page means something specific - this lesson walks through the fields one by one so you stop reading numbers you cannot explain.

A block explorer is not a wallet, an exchange or an authority. It is a searchable index that reads the public ledger and lays one account or one transaction out on a page so a human can read it. That distinction matters, because everything trustworthy on that page is just a faithful copy of data that already exists on the chain - and everything you should be cautious about is any place the explorer adds its own interpretation. The right posture is to treat the page as a window, verify the view, and never confuse the window with the room.

A block explorer reports from its own index of the chain, and that index can be stale, can mis-render a value, or can be an operator's copy rather than the ground truth. The fix is cheap and mechanical: paste the same hash into a second, independent explorer for the same network, or query a node directly, and confirm the block number and status agree. Two unrelated sources landing on the same answer is what turns "the page says" into "the chain says." A single confident screenshot, by contrast, remains exactly what it is - one opinion rendered as an image.
A boundary that follows the highest recorded equity upward and never returns down.

A chain cannot see the world, so on-chain finance borrows prices from an oracle or index feed and trusts the result. Everything downstream - mark prices, collateral valuations, liquidation triggers - is only as correct as that borrowed input. When the feed is stale or wrong, immutability becomes a liability: the mistaken liquidation is now permanent and perfectly verifiable. That is the most common way on-chain transparency misleads - you admire how tamper-proof the recorded price is while nothing checks whether it was true.
A challenge is not a profit contest but a screening device for loss behaviour, and each published model screens with a different combination of target, limit and activity requirement.

A classic futures contract expires: on a set day it converges to the spot price and closes. A perpetual drops that date, so it could drift away from reality at any moment. To stop this, the venue runs a payment between longs and shorts — the funding rate — that rewards whichever side is helping pull the contract price back toward the market.

A consistency rule caps the share of total profit that a single best day may account for, so a result cannot rest on one lucky spike. It is usually written as a percentage: if the cap were 35%, no day could exceed 35% of cumulative profit. The exact percentage differs by firm and by plan; Openfund publishes its own challenge conditions on its rulebook page, and paid activation, funded accounts and payouts are not enabled in this release.

A credible reserves report is built so that an outsider can re-check it rather than take it on faith. The usual mechanism signs a message from the addresses themselves, or publishes a Merkle tree whose leaves are individual balances and whose published root lets each holder confirm their own line without seeing anyone else's. Both designs answer the same question - can you independently confirm that these assets exist at these addresses - and both stop there. Nothing in the mechanism compels the publisher to reveal every address it controls, or anything it does not control on-chain.

A funded account is the stage a prop programme places you on after an evaluation - or, in some models, without one. It is a trading account whose terms are written so that the account size is provided under the agreement while you trade it, and the profit you produce is shared rather than kept whole. None of that makes it a deposit account in your own name: what you receive is a set of conditions, and the conditions are the product.

A high-water mark is the best recorded equity or balance level, and it never moves down

A high-water mark is the highest account value the record has ever reached. Drawdown is measured downward from this peak, and profit-based limits — for example a trailing drawdown — often rise with it. Depending on the rule, the mark may update on equity or only on closed balance, and it may or may not reset after a payout, so the definition matters and differs by venue.

A limit order states the worst price you will accept and rests in the book until the market reaches it. It guarantees the price but not the fill: in a fast or thin market it may fill only partly or not at all. Resting limit orders add liquidity and usually earn the lower maker fee, unlike market orders that take liquidity.

A losing trade that followed the plan is not the problem - it is an expected expense of a process whose edge appears only across many trades. The problem is the ninety seconds after the loss prints: the tightening in the chest, the wish to be instantly back to even, and a new decision made by someone who is no longer the person who placed it. Most of the money traders lose beyond their statistics is lost in that window, not to the market but to the reaction.
A loss limit that follows a rising high-water mark instead of a fixed value.

A maker fee is charged when your order rests in the book and is later taken by someone else, adding liquidity rather than removing it. Venues set it below the taker fee to reward orders that deepen the book. The exact rate, and whether makers pay anything at all, differ by exchange and often by volume tier.
A margin mode that pools collateral across all positions in the account.

A market order executes at once by taking whatever the order book offers until its size is filled, trading a guaranteed fill for no guaranteed price. Because it removes resting liquidity it pays the higher taker fee, and a large market order in a thin book walks several price levels, producing slippage. Use it when getting in or out matters more than the exact print.

A market order removes liquidity: it takes whatever the book offers until your size is filled, which is why a large market order can clear several levels. A limit order adds liquidity when it rests: you set the worst price you accept and let someone else come to you, trading a guaranteed price for the chance of no fill at all.

A perpetual future is a contract between two traders that settles against the price of an underlying asset — crypto, an index, a commodity — without ever fixing a date to deliver it. You do not own the asset; you hold a position whose value rises when the price moves in your favour and falls when it moves against you.

A perpetual future is a leveraged, collateralised contract that settles against an underlying price but has no expiry date, so you can hold it indefinitely. With no delivery date to force convergence, it relies on the funding rate between longs and shorts to keep its price near the index. You never own the underlying asset; you hold a position whose value tracks the price up or down.
A perpetual is a leveraged contract on price with no delivery date

A perpetual venue shows you more than one price for the same asset, and confusing them is a common source of surprise. One is a neutral reference built from outside markets; the other is the price the venue itself uses to value your position. They usually sit close, and when they do not, that difference matters.

A single trade is too small a sample to say anything about a decision, which is why the checklist ends with a yes-or-no on plan-followed rather than a grade on profit. Over a batch of trades that all followed one rule, the honest score is expectancy: it folds the win rate and the average size of winners and losers into the one number a repeated decision is actually worth.

A smart contract is program code deployed on a blockchain that carries out predefined rules automatically when its conditions are met, with its logic and storage visible on-chain. Anyone can read the deployed bytecode and events, but visible code is not the same as verified or safe: it may be unverified on an explorer, upgradeable through a proxy, or hold privileges that let it change balances. Treat a contract behaviour as exactly what its published, verified source shows — nothing more.

A static floor from the starting size is the friendliest of the three: you can lose the same distance again after a recovery, because the line does not move. A trailing boundary is the opposite - every new best equity raises it, so a rising account trades with progressively less room below. On the Instant terms of record the total drawdown trails at 5%, then locks at breakeven once the account is 5% in profit, and it does not reset after a payout. That shape rewards early restraint and punishes the instinct to size up after a good run.

A stop is only useful if it was placed while you were calm and left in place while you are not. Write down the level and the reason for it, then let the order do the job you have already decided on.

A stop order does nothing until its trigger price is touched; then it becomes a market or limit order. A stop-loss turns into a seller into the book when you are wrong, which protects you but also means the exit price is not fixed in a fast or thin market — a gap can fill far from your trigger.
A stop-loss converts an open-ended loss into a defined one, but only if the trigger, the order type and the level behind them were decided before the trade hurt.

A stop-loss is a decision taken before you are in pain: the price at which you accept that the reason for the trade has expired and step out. It does not guarantee a good exit. Its value is that it turns an open-ended loss into a defined one, chosen by you in a calm moment instead of by the market in its worst hour.

A stop-loss is a trigger you set in advance that closes a position once the price reaches a defined loss level, converting into a market or limit order at that point. It caps how far a single trade can hurt you, but because the triggered order then enters the market, the exit price is not guaranteed: in a gap or a fast move the fill can be worse than your stop. Where and how tightly to place it — manual versus a hard order, and which price the trigger reads — depend on the venue rules.
A stop-market guarantees exit and not price; a stop-limit protects price and may leave you holding
A stop-out is one trade away

A take-profit is a trigger set in advance that closes a position once the price reaches a chosen gain level, locking in the result without you having to act. Like a stop-loss it turns into an order at its trigger, so a limit take-profit may fill only if price actually reaches it and a market take-profit fills at whatever is available. Placing it too close surrenders upside; the distance between take-profit and stop-loss sets the trade reward-to-risk ratio.

A taker fee is charged when your order crosses the spread and matches existing resting orders, removing liquidity from the book. Venues price it above the maker fee to discourage draining depth. Market orders are the typical taker, but any resting order you lift pays the taker fee too, and the exact rate varies by exchange and volume tier.

Transparency at this layer is not about pretty charts; it is whether you can reach the actual program that decides your balance.

Its value comes entirely from consistency of recording: once the fields drift from trade to trade, every metric derived from them drifts too and the record quietly turns into decoration. The goal here is the smallest schema that still produces real metrics.

Balance is the total cash credited to an account: the money added, plus realized profit and loss and any charged fees. It ignores open positions, so it only changes when a trade closes or a fee is taken. Equity is balance plus the floating PnL of open positions, so the two differ while you hold something.

Basis is the difference between the perpetual own price and the index price it tracks. A positive basis means the contract trades above the reference; a negative basis means it trades below. Mark price is usually built as the index price plus a bounded, smoothed basis, and funding is what pulls that basis back toward zero.

Because there is no expiry to force convergence, a perpetual relies on funding. When the contract trades above the reference price, most traders are long, and longs pay shorts; when it trades below, shorts pay longs. That payment is a cost of holding the popular side, so it nudges positioning and price back toward the underlying.

Cross margin lends the free equity of the account to every open position at once

Cross margin lets every open position draw on the same shared balance as collateral, so profitable or free positions cushion losing ones. It lowers each position liquidation price because more equity backs it, but it links their risk: one severe move can consume the whole balance and liquidate everything at once. Isolated margin is the alternative that ring-fences collateral to a single position.
Cross margin: one buffer for everyone

Cross mode pools the free equity of the account behind every open position at once, so a losing trade is measured against the whole balance and can absorb far more adverse movement before it is closed. That is also the danger: a position that would have died quietly in isolation now draws collateral out of the account, and in a fast market several positions can consume the shared buffer together. When the pool runs out, everything resting on it is liquidated, not just the trade that began it.

Discipline becomes a routine you run rather than a mood you feel. Before the order you confirm the three numbers and that the setup sentence is true. While the position is open you act only on what was written; anything new is a fresh decision for the next session, made cold. After it closes you record whether you followed the plan and tag what you felt, so the journal can separate rule-following losses from impulsive ones - worth very different things over a sample even when the money column is identical.

Discipline is judging a decision by the information available when you made it, not by the profit it happened to print; a pre-trade checklist and a written plan are how a trader makes that separation concrete.

Discipline means many things, but for a process it means one: evaluate a decision on the facts you had when you made it, and refuse to let the result rewrite that verdict. Traders who judge every closed trade by its profit or loss learn the wrong lesson half the time - a sound plan stopped out on a random spike printed a loss, an impulsive lucky bet printed a win. Reward the bet and punish the plan and you slowly train yourself to be worse. The checklist exists to break that loop.

Open interest is the total number or value of contracts that remain open. Every long must be matched by a short, so it counts both sides and never favours one: rising open interest with price signals new money entering, while falling open interest signals positions being closed. It measures how crowded a market is, not which way it will move, and not every data feed exposes it.

Open interest is the total of contracts still open. Because every long needs a matching short, it never favours one side. Rising open interest alongside price says new money is entering; falling open interest says positions are being closed. It measures crowding, not direction — the same way funding measures which side is paying.

Position size is the amount — units or notional value — you commit to one trade. In risk-based sizing you choose it so that the distance to your stop-loss costs a fixed fraction of the account, which makes the loss per trade the controllable variable rather than the market. Risk of ruin is the probability that losses drive an account to a point from which it can no longer keep trading. It grows with per-trade risk and with how negative or thin your edge is, and shrinks as the bankroll grows relative to each bet. It is a statistical estimate under explicit model assumptions — fixed bet size, a given win rate and independent trades — so a low figure is not a guarantee, and a change in behaviour can invalidate the model.

Risk of ruin is the probability that losses take you to a point where you can no longer trade. It is built from win rate, average win and loss, risk per trade and a chosen ruin threshold, and it rests on assumptions markets routinely break: independent trades, a constant edge, an unchanging risk fraction, no effect from gaps or funding. Read it as a conditional estimate, never a guarantee.

Risk per unit is the distance from entry to stop, reward per unit the distance from entry to target; their ratio is the reward-to-risk figure. Planned money at risk comes from account equity × risk percentage, and the planned reward scales by the same ratio. With a win rate supplied, expectancy is p × average win − (1 − p) × average loss, expressed in money and in R multiples. The break-even win rate is risk ÷ (risk + reward); a fee-adjusted version treats the round-trip cost as extra risk.

Run it once and it stays with you. Lose 20% of 10,000 and you are left with 8,000. Returning to 10,000 means earning 2,000 on 8,000, which is 25%. Lose half and the required gain is 100%. The relation is convex, so the first few percent of loss are cheap and the deep ones are almost unaffordable. That, not discipline for its own sake, is the real argument for cutting a loss early — while the arithmetic is still on your side.

Slippage is the difference between the price you expected when you placed an order and the average price you were actually filled at. It grows when your size is large relative to order-book depth or when the market moves fast, because a market order must then walk more levels. Limit orders and smaller, split entries reduce it, but a fill can then be partial or missed instead.

Slippage is the difference between the price you saw when you decided and the average you actually got. It grows with your size relative to depth and with speed: a thin book or a fast move forces a market order to walk further down the ladder. Using limit orders, splitting size, or trading calmer hours reduces it, but never removes it.

The Kelly criterion gives the fraction of capital that maximises the expected long-run logarithmic growth rate of the account. In its simple form the fraction is f = (p·b − q) / b, where p is win rate, q its complement and b the win-to-loss ratio. Full Kelly is the mathematically aggressive extreme: it assumes your edge estimates are accurate, so most practitioners bet a fraction of it — half Kelly or less — to tolerate estimation error and avoid ruin.

The Kelly criterion gives the fraction of equity that maximises long-run growth when your probability and payoff estimates are correct. Treat it as a ceiling rather than a target. Its inputs come from a finite sample, the true edge is usually flatter than the measured one, and full Kelly on an overestimated edge is the standard route to the ruin above. Fractional Kelly exists to price that error.

The funding rate is a periodic payment exchanged between traders holding opposite sides — longs and shorts — not a fee paid to the exchange. The funding rate is the mechanism that keeps a perpetual honest. Its job is simple: make it expensive to crowd onto whichever side is already pushing the contract away from the underlying price.

The last limit sits between two claims that sound similar. Code-level transparency means anyone can read the repository, the build, the deployed contracts and their verified sources; it is concrete, checkable and increasingly standard. Financial transparency is different - proof of reserves, an independent audit of your own contracts, a settlement layer you can verify. Neither follows from the other: a project can publish flawless open-source code and still have no reserves proof, no audit of itself and no customer funds on-chain.

The last step is the one people skip: separating the confirmed on-chain facts from the story attached to them. The ledger can confirm that value moved from address A to address B at block N - it cannot confirm that the transaction represents a payment, a settlement, a customer balance or a promise. Those meanings are added around the data by whatever report or UI handed you the hash. Verification ends at the chain; interpretation beyond it is a claim to be checked against other evidence, not a fact the explorer owes you.

Verification is not a feeling of confidence you get after reading a long receipt. It is a short procedure you can run yourself in a couple of minutes, and the discipline of running it - especially when the narrative is flattering - is the whole point. The procedure assumes nothing about who gave you the hash; it starts from that string and ends at an independent confirmation, with a checklist in between. The moment you can describe it as a sequence of actions rather than a mood, you have left marketing behind.

Verification is worth understanding precisely because it is narrower than it sounds. When an explorer marks a contract "verified," someone has published source code whose compiled bytecode matches what is deployed at that address. That is a real service: it lets you read the logic instead of guessing from transactions. But it says nothing about whether the logic is honest, reviewed, or will stay unchanged. A verified contract can contain a self-destruct, and an unverified one might be perfectly ordinary.

Your inputs are converted into the mean and the variance of per-trade returns at the chosen risk fraction. The estimate then applies the standard diffusion approximation, P ≈ exp(−2 × mean × ln(capital ÷ stop-out level) ÷ variance). Alongside it you get the per-trade edge, the Kelly fraction for these inputs, and the largest risk fraction that keeps the estimated probability below 5%.
